morning.title: EviPathBench: Benchmarking Evidence Acquisition and Reasoning in Vision-Language Models for Whole-Slide Pathology
morning.text:
arXiv:2607.19261v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Whole-slide image (WSI) diagnosis requires identifying diagnostically relevant regions, examining them across magnifications, and integrating multi-scale evidence. However, most pathology benchmarks evaluate models on pre-cropped patches or pre-extracted slide features, leaving their ability to acquire evidence from gigapixel WSIs largely untested. We introduce EviPathBench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence acquisition and reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) for whole-slide pathology. It evaluates four capabilities: image-to-text matching for evidence interpretation, text-to-image retrieval for evidence verification, diagnostic-region localization for evidence acquisition, and multi-scale reasoning for evidence integration. The benchmark is organized as a diagnostic tree linking nested regions across magnifications with scale-specific findings and path-level diagnoses. It contains 1,822 TCGA WSIs and 17,135 diagnostic paths annotated by ten board-certified pathologists. A private cohort of 190 breast cancer WSIs with detailed annotations further evaluates autonomous whole-slide exploration. We evaluate 19 VLMs spanning general-purpose, medical, and pathology-specialized families, plus one text-only reference model. Leading open-weight models achieve over 93% accuracy in multi-scale reasoning and over 50% in both cross-modal matching tasks. In contrast, diagnostic-region localization remains challenging: the best text-guided mean intersection-over-union is below 0.09, underperforming a center-based heuristic. During autonomous exploration, the unconditional hit rate drops from 0.522 at low magnification to 0.185 at intermediate magnification and 0.020 at high magnification. These results reveal a pronounced gap between reasoning over curated evidence and acquiring it from WSIs. EviPathBench provides a unified framework for measuring and improving both capabilities.

morning.title: DELE-w0.5: Inferring Action from Future Latent State for Robotic Manipulation
morning.text:
arXiv:2608.22067v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) build robot control on video-generation backbones, which jointly predict dense future visual trajectories and robot actions. We argue that video generation is an unnecessary intermediate objective for world-action modeling. For robotic manipulation, the goal of a world model is not to reproduce how the world looks at every intermediate moment, but to predict the state that the world will reach after an action is executed. The intermediate frames only describe the visual transition between physical states, which consumes substantial model capacity and computation, but do not directly specify the physical outcome that the robot action is intended to produce. In this paper, we propose DELE-w0.5, which infers robot actions from predicted future states without relying on video generation. Concretely, DELE-w0.5 infers the action sequence from its corresponding compact future latent state. The future latent state captures the action-relevant physical outcome of robot interaction and serves as an explicit bridge between world modeling and action generation. The core design principle of DELE-w0.5 is to model how the physical world changes under robot actions, rather than how its visual appearance evolves frame by frame. This formulation removes the high-dimensional visual redundancy introduced by dense video representations, and it therefore enables cheaper training and low-latency inference. Across 480 real-robot trials on four long-horizon manipulation tasks, our DELE-w0.5 achieves the best performance among all compared policies, attaining 62.5 overall full-task success and 81.3 macro ordered-stage progress, outperforming the strongest baseline by 47.5 and 30.7 percentage points, respectively.

morning.title: AeroDPO: Unleashing Lightweight UAV Navigation with High-Fidelity Perception and Automated Preference Optimization
morning.text:
arXiv:2608.07557v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV-VLN) requires rapid and reactive control in complex 3D environments. Recent minimalist end-to-end paradigms show great promise but typically rely on massive language models containing billions of parameters, incurring prohibitive latency for real-world edge deployment. In this paper, we challenge this parameter-heavy reliance. Comprehensive cross-scale evaluations reveal the critical insight that perception quality fundamentally outweighs language reasoning capacity. We demonstrate that a lightweight 2B model equipped with high-fidelity visual inputs completely matches the overall success rates of massive 7B baselines. However, this minimalist policy exposes a fundamental robustness flaw inherent to pure Behavior Cloning (BC). Lacking explicit negative feedback, the agent fails to internalize robust spatial constraints and exhibits alarming collision rates in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. To overcome this vulnerability without relying on unscalable human annotations, we propose AeroDPO, a zero-cost automated Direct Preference Optimization pipeline driven by deterministic physical simulation state rollback. Upon detecting collisions, the system autonomously rewinds the environment to extract causal reasoning errors as rejected actions, applies decoupled privileged interventions to synthesize collision-avoidance preferred maneuvers, and leverages an offline vision language inspector to filter visual ambiguities. By equipping our 2B model with this automated data flywheel, AeroDPO boosts success rates to 49.16% on unmapped scenarios while drastically suppressing collision rates, establishing a new SOTA for autonomous aerial agents.

India Plans Long-Range LR-AShM Upgrade to Strike Aircraft Carriers Up to 3,500 km Away
morning.text:
According to sources close to idrw.org, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is looking into a future longer-range version of the Long Range Anti-Ship Missile (LR-AShM), the possible range being raised from the currently reported baseline of about 1,500 km to roughly 3,500 km. Should this variant be developed, it would mark a significant broadening of the missile’s role, extending its use beyond traditional coastal anti-ship operations to include a strategic long-range maritime strike capability.
This reported advancement will be based on the LR-AShM’s current boost-glide design. It is a hypersonic system being developed for the Indian Navy and is meant to give it the ability to engage targets at long range from a maritime position. Previously, DRDO has referred to the LR-AShM as a hypersonic glide missile capable of attacking both stationary and moving targets and of carrying various payloads.
If the missile’s range was to be extended to about 3,500 km, it would take much more than just increasing the quantity of propellant. All of the missile’s propulsion system, aerodynamic shape, thermal protection, guidance system and flight profile would have to be adapted to handle a greatly increased mission duration.
A possible way forward would be to use higher-energy solid propulsion and to optimise the boost phase. The booster must give the hypersonic glide vehicle enough initial speed and altitude before releasing it on its extended-range flight path. It therefore makes sense to regard changes to the propellant formulation, motor efficiency and stage configuration as important areas for research, although the exact design of any future LR-AShM variant is still not disclosed.
The hypersonic glide vehicle would then play a crucial role in attaining the extra range; rather than travelling through the air along a normal ballistic path, a boost-glide system can make use of aerodynamic lift as it moves through the upper atmosphere. A future long-range LR-AShM might well adopt a carefully optimised trajectory in order to keep a high velocity over a considerably greater distance.
Thermal management would become the main challenge. When a vehicle travels at hypersonic speed for a long time, it suffers from serious aerodynamic heating. If the weapon is to remain manoeuvrable during a flight of 3,500 km, advanced thermal-protection materials, better high-temperature structures and aerodynamic optimisation would therefore be necessary.
Navigation would also pose a major challenge. At these distances, minor errors which accumulate during the boost and glide stages can result in considerable deviations in position. The system of the future would thus have to make use of a highly resilient navigation architecture that combines accurate inertial navigation with assistance from satellite navigation and possibly other autonomous navigation methods.
India’s NavIC might be used as part of such an architecture, and advanced ring-laser or fibre-optic inertial sensors could ensure continued navigation when satellite signals are not available or are deliberately blocked. The system would have to be capable of carrying out its mission even in difficult electronic-warfare situations.
If the 3,500-km programme moves forward, the strategic consequences would be important. A missile of that range would enable India to place distant maritime areas at risk from launch sites on land, and might therefore result in a significantly wider anti-access/area-denial zone around the Indian coastline and around its strategically important island territories.
It could also be used to supplement rather than to replace existing systems such as BrahMos; BrahMos offers a mature capability for supersonic cruise missiles, while a future long-range LR-AShM could provide a hypersonic boost-glide option with a much greater range, making it more difficult for an adversary to predict and defend against India’s maritime strike capabilities.
The 3,500-km range mentioned should at this time be seen as a development goal, not an officially confirmed operational specification, since DRDO has not yet made a public announcement of an operational LR-AShM model with that range, and a great deal of further development and testing would have to take place before such a capability could be deployed.
Even if it is successful, the programme could still be one of India’s most important future developments in long-range missiles, especially since the Indian Navy is placing increasing emphasis on keeping hostile surface forces at a distance and on establishing a distributed maritime strike network.

morning.title: DRDO Confirms Work on Shoulder-Fired SF-VSHORADS Missile for Indian Armed Forces
morning.text:
India’s air defence modernisation programme is moving into its next phase, with the Defence Research and Development Organisation confirming that it is working on a shoulder-fired variant of its indigenous Very Short-Range Air Defence System, a configuration that would let a single soldier fire the missile directly off the shoulder without the tripod mount that was required in the current system.
The baseline VSHORADS, developed by DRDO’s Research Centre Imarat in Hyderabad in collaboration with other DRDO laboratories and development-cum-production partners, is a fourth-generation man-portable air-defence system designed to counter low-altitude threats such as drones, helicopters and fast-moving aircraft. The missile itself weighs roughly 20.5 kilograms and carries a dual-band imaging infrared seeker capable of engaging targets between 250 metres and 6 kilometres, at altitudes up to 3.5 kilometres, travelling at speeds up to Mach 1.5. In its current form, however, the system requires a tripod-mounted launcher and sighting unit that brings the total deployed weight closer to 40 kilograms, a configuration well suited to static defensive positions along high-altitude picket lines but far less practical for infantry units that need to move quickly and engage on the move.
The tripod variant has already cleared a string of validation milestones. Three consecutive flight trials were carried out from the Integrated Test Range at Chandipur in February 2026, with the missiles intercepting and destroying high-speed targets simulating enemy aircraft across a range of engagement scenarios, in the presence of representatives from all three armed services. Those tests followed earlier developmental trials at the Pokhran Field Firing Ranges in October 2024 and at Chandipur in February 2025, each aimed at revalidating hit-to-kill performance against threats flying at varying speed, range and altitude. With developmental testing of the tripod configuration now largely complete and the system entering user trials with the Indian Army, DRDO’s attention has shifted to the harder engineering problem of shrinking the weapon down to a true shoulder-launched form factor.
That shift was acknowledged in Parliament, where the Minister of State for Defence stated that the technologies and several subsystems developed for VSHORADS can be repurposed for a dedicated shoulder-fired indigenous air defence missile. The goal is to bring the missile’s own weight down from around 21 kilograms to somewhere in the 15 to 18 kilogram range, placing it in the same class as established shoulder-fired systems such as the American Stinger and the Russian Verba, while retaining the roughly 6-kilometre engagement envelope of the parent system. Achieving that reduction is expected to require a redesigned, more compact rocket motor and a miniaturised seeker assembly, since simply stripping the tripod away from the existing missile would leave it too heavy and too long for a soldier to comfortably shoulder-fire and reload in the field.
If DRDO succeeds, the resulting SF-VSHORADS would give Indian infantry, including units operating in mountainous terrain along the northern and western borders, a genuinely portable answer to low-flying aerial threats without sacrificing the imaging infrared guidance and target-discrimination capability that distinguishes VSHORADS from third-generation systems like the Stinger. It would also directly address the operational gap left by India’s ageing Igla and Igla-1M inventory, MANPADS that have been in service since the 1980s and are increasingly outmatched by modern drone swarms and low-signature aerial targets.

morning.title: Tejas MkII Unlikely to Appear at Aero India 2027
morning.text:
According to sources close to the Tejas MkII programme, idrw.org has found that the aircraft is not expected to be physically present at Aero India 2027, despite an increasing expectation that it could become one of the main highlights of the event. The main reason for this is the anticipated timing of the aircraft’s first flight and the site where its development and flight-testing are taking place.
Aero India 2027 is set to take place at Air Force Station Yelahanka in Bengaluru in February 2027. While the Indian Air Force has confirmed Bengaluru as the site for the 16th edition, the exact dates had still not been announced as of early August. Sources who are familiar with the programme indicate that the first flight of the Tejas MkII is now expected to occur around July 2027, on the basis that the current work on the prototype, including integration, ground testing and certification, continues in accordance with the revised schedule. This would mean that the aircraft’s first flight takes place about five months after Aero India 2027.
The fact that the event takes place at that time presents a major logistical problem if the aircraft are to be on display.
The development of the Tejas MkII is being carried out by HAL’s LCA Division, and the production and development work of this division is not based at the Yelahanka Air Force Station. Since Yelahanka is in northern Bengaluru and has in the past hosted Aero India, the flight-testing and manufacturing activities for the Tejas programme are situated somewhere else in the city. It would therefore be necessary either to transport the aircraft by road or to carry out a flight before its official first flight if an unflown prototype were to be moved from its development facility to Yelahanka.
If the first flight is still scheduled for July, then the latter option would obviously be impossible.
In principle it is technically feasible to transport a large fighter prototype by road, but in order to get an unflown development aircraft to an airshow it would be necessary to carry out considerable preparation, disassembly, use specialised transport and then reassemble it. More importantly, however, the arrangement would provide only limited value since the aircraft is still many months away from its first flight.
It makes it much more likely that the Tejas MkII will be on display at Aero India 2027 in the form of a mock-up or a full-scale static model than as the actual flying prototype.
The fact also shows just how different the Tejas MkII programme is from the usual expectations associated with an airshow debut, since earlier Aero India events have often been used for displaying new aircraft and prototypes and it was therefore expected that the MkII should also make an appearance at the next one.
The programme’s present main concern is first-flight readiness not airshow presentation.
The Tejas MkII prototype has already got as far as an advanced stage in terms of manufacturing and integration, but it must still carry out the required ground checks, go through the flight-clearance procedures and complete the related preparations before it can start flight testing. Various first-flight dates have been given in the public reports, which shows how uncertain the programme’s schedule is.
Should the timeline for July 2027 as provided by the sources prove to be correct, the first public flight of the Tejas MkII might then turn into a considerably more important event at a later date in 2027.
The first flight of the aircraft will be a significant achievement for India’s fighter-development programme since the MkII is meant to fill the capabilities gap between the lighter Tejas Mk1A and the much larger AMCA; it is anticipated to offer greater range, payload and internal fuel capacity together with a more powerful sensor and weapons system.
As a result, the Tejas MkII might be shown at Aero India 2027 through scale models, displays and programme briefings, but the actual event could be several months later when the prototype finally flies.
At this stage, the planned first flight in July 2027 should be regarded as information based on sources and not as an officially confirmed date; the timeline could be altered if the programme progresses more quickly, or else additional testing or certification requirements could cause the first flight to be postponed beyond July.

morning.title: DRDO Eyes Rydberg Quantum Sensors for GPS-Jam-Resistant Navigation and Electronic Warfare
morning.text:
India’s defence research establishment is placing an early bet on atomic-scale physics to solve one of the most persistent vulnerabilities in modern warfare: the ease with which GPS signals can be jammed or spoofed, and the blind spots that conventional radio receivers leave in contested electromagnetic environments.
At the centre of this push is a set of tenders awarded by Research Centre Imarat, a premier laboratory under the Defence Research and Development Organisation, to Bengaluru-based quantum technology firm QuBeats. The two multi-crore contracts cover the development of a Rydberg-based Quantum RF Sensor and a separate Quantum Gyroscope, both representing frontier applications of quantum-enabled sensing rather than incremental upgrades to existing electronic warfare hardware. Both systems are expected to move through rigorous development and testing phases before any eventual integration into operational defence platforms, and DRDO’s approach of engaging an industry partner directly reflects an effort to compress the usual gap between laboratory-scale quantum research and deployable military systems.
The physics underpinning the RF sensor is what sets it apart from anything currently fielded by India’s forces. Rydberg atoms are atoms whose outer electrons have been excited by lasers to extremely high energy levels, a state that makes them exceptionally sensitive to surrounding electromagnetic fields. When an incoming radio signal interacts with atoms held in this excited state inside a sealed glass vapour cell, it perturbs their energy levels in a way that can be read out optically rather than through a conventional antenna and receiver circuit. This electromagnetically induced transparency effect allows the sensor to register RF signals with SI-traceable precision across an unusually broad slice of spectrum, from the low-frequency bands used by legacy communications equipment up toward the higher frequencies associated with modern radar and satellite links. The glass cell itself, the sealed chamber holding the atomic vapour under laser excitation, effectively functions as the entire receiver, replacing the bulky antenna arrays and tuned circuitry that classical RF systems depend on.
The strategic appeal for India is straightforward. GPS jamming and spoofing have become routine features of contested airspace and maritime environments worldwide, and conventional satellite navigation receivers have no inherent defence against a sufficiently powerful jamming signal overwhelming the faint GPS transmission arriving from orbit. A Rydberg-based receiver, by contrast, does not rely on decoding a specific weak signal the way a GPS chipset does; its atomic sensing medium can be tuned across a wide band and is comparatively resistant to the kind of brute-force interference that defeats antenna-based systems. Parallel programmes pursuing similar physics have been reported by defence-linked quantum sensing firms internationally, alongside heavy investment from agencies such as DARPA and the US Army Research Laboratory, underscoring that India’s entry into this space places it alongside a small group of countries actively racing to militarise Rydberg atom sensing.
The companion Quantum Gyroscope programme addresses a related but distinct problem: sustaining accurate navigation once GPS is denied altogether. Where the RF sensor is built to detect and characterise signals in a contested spectrum, a quantum gyroscope is designed to track a platform’s orientation and rotation with far greater precision and lower drift than conventional fibre-optic or ring-laser gyroscopes, offering a path toward reliable dead-reckoning navigation over extended missions without any external signal at all.
Both efforts remain in early development, and DRDO’s own framing treats them as long-horizon technology bets rather than near-term inductions. But the direction is unambiguous: India is trying to build sovereign quantum-sensing capability before GPS-denial and spectrum-contested warfare become the default operating environment rather than the exception.

morning.title: Pakistan Mislocated Indian Carrier Battle Group by 300 Nautical Miles, Says Gen Anil Chauhan
morning.text:
General Anil Chauhan, former Chief of Defence Staff, has given a clear assessment of Pakistan’s intelligence and situational awareness during Operation Sindoor, noting that Islamabad’s knowledge of Indian military activities was especially poor in the maritime domain.
At a recent meeting devoted to the 2025 conflict, General Chauhan stated that the Pakistani daily military briefings consistently gave the position of an Indian carrier battle group in the Arabian Sea. Yet, when the Indian side compared those reported positions with the information obtained from the Western Naval Command, it was found that the true position of the carrier group was said to be between 100 and 300 nautical miles from the position stated in the Pakistani briefings.
The previous CDS stated that Pakistan’s general understanding of the maritime situation was “quite poor”, which casts doubt on the quality and independence of the intelligence information provided to Islamabad during the conflict. As Gen. Chauhan pointed out, there were two possible reasons: Pakistan might be getting incorrect information regarding the Indian carrier battle group, or it might be placing great reliance on foreign intelligence sources who themselves were not able to give accurately timely information.
The most notable aspect of his evaluation was the fact that Pakistan’s maritime surveillance aircraft “did not fly at all” during that period, which in turn restricted its capacity to independently keep an eye on the movements of Indian naval forces in the Arabian Sea.
It would have led to a large intelligence gap. Since a carrier battle group is a highly mobile unit, it is necessary to use a combination of maritime patrol aircraft, satellites, electronic intelligence, surface surveillance, submarines and other intelligence sources in order to locate it accurately. Relying too much on a single external source or on a outdated intelligence picture could result in exactly the kind of positional errors that Gen. Chauhan described.
The situation is especially significant since India sent in a large number of naval forces during the crisis. According to open-source reports, an Indian carrier battle group based on the INS Vikrant operated in the Arabian Sea together with a bigger surface fleet. The purpose of this deployment was not simply to engage in conventional maritime combat but also to apply strategic pressure by showing that India was capable of threatening Pakistani maritime and coastal targets.
It would therefore have been important for Pakistan to accurately track the Indian fleet if it was to get a clear idea of the possible direction and extent of any escalation. If the maritime situation were inaccurate then the naval forces would be obliged to operate more cautiously and valuable assets might as a result be kept away from areas in which the Indian forces could have been able to strike.
This scene also shows how important maritime domain awareness (MDA) is becoming in today’s warfare. Warfare at sea is not any longer just about one ship spotting another; it is increasingly the satellites, the long-range UAVs, the maritime patrol aircraft, the electronic intelligence, the undersea sensors and the networked command systems that decide who has the better picture of the battlespace.
For India, General Chauhan’s remarks offer a significant clue as to the fact that its maritime deception and the way it distributed its forces may have made Pakistan’s intelligence situation more difficult during Operation Sindoor. Yet his evaluation cannot be simply seen as proof that Pakistan had no knowledge of the Indian naval movements. The information available only shows that the positions mentioned in the Pakistani briefings were reported to be considerably inaccurate.
The main point is that in a high-intensity conflict situational awareness can be just as important as having weapons; for example, a navy which has powerful missiles but which does not have an accurate knowledge of where its adversary is located will have difficulty in using those weapons effectively. On the other hand, a force that is able to keep a reliable picture of the situation while at the same time hiding its own movements can achieve a significant operational advantage.

morning.title: From Mirage F1 Rejection to Mirage 2000 ‘Vajra’: How India Found Its Iconic Fighter
morning.text:
India’s relationship with Dassault fighter aircraft could have begun with the Mirage F1, decades before the Mirage 2000 became one of the Indian Air Force’s most successful combat aircraft. In the 1970s, France offered the Mirage F1 to India during the IAF’s search for a Deep Penetration Strike Aircraft (DPSA), but the aircraft was reportedly rejected after an Indian evaluation team concluded that it did not fully satisfy the service’s demanding requirements.
The episode provides an interesting example of how India’s fighter-acquisition decisions have sometimes been shaped less by the aircraft’s overall reputation and more by the specific mission for which it was being evaluated. During the early 1970s, the IAF was looking for an aircraft capable of conducting deep strikes against targets well inside enemy territory while carrying a substantial weapons load. The requirement called for an aircraft capable of carrying roughly two tonnes of ordnance at high speed while penetrating approximately 250 nautical miles into hostile territory.
An IAF evaluation team led by Air Marshal Y.V. Malse travelled to France to examine the Mirage F1 and reportedly conducted flight evaluations of the aircraft. Despite the Mirage F1’s impressive performance for its generation, the aircraft did not fully satisfy the Indian requirements for the DPSA role.
The decision was significant because the Mirage F1 was already emerging as a capable multirole combat aircraft internationally. France had developed it as a successor to the Mirage III family, with a swept-wing configuration rather than the delta-wing design that would later become synonymous with the Mirage 2000.
For India’s particular requirement, however, the aircraft’s payload-range characteristics reportedly fell short of what the IAF wanted from its deep-strike platform.
The DPSA competition ultimately resulted in the selection of the SEPECAT Jaguar, an Anglo-French strike aircraft specifically suited to the deep-penetration mission. The Jaguar’s combination of low-level performance, weapons payload and range made it a better match for India’s requirements.
The story could have ended there, with the Mirage family rejected by the IAF. Instead, France returned with a considerably more advanced proposition.
By the late 1970s, Dassault was aggressively promoting the Mirage 2000, a new-generation fighter incorporating a delta-wing configuration, fly-by-wire flight controls and substantially improved avionics and performance. Unlike the Mirage F1, the Mirage 2000 was not being positioned simply as a deep-strike aircraft. Its design offered India a broader multirole capability.
India eventually selected the Mirage 2000, with the first contract signed in 1982. The aircraft entered IAF service as the Mirage 2000H/TH, later receiving the Indian name Vajra.
The decision would prove particularly important for the IAF.
The Mirage 2000 subsequently became one of India’s most respected combat aircraft, demonstrating its value in both conventional warfare and precision-strike missions. During the 1999 Kargil War, Mirage 2000s were extensively employed for precision attacks against Pakistani positions at high altitude.
Two decades later, the aircraft again became central to an Indian precision-strike operation when Mirage 2000s were used in the 2019 Balakot airstrikes.
The evolution from Mirage F1 rejection to Mirage 2000 induction is therefore an interesting case of how India’s requirements changed alongside aviation technology. The aircraft that did not satisfy India’s DPSA requirement in the 1970s was followed by a significantly more advanced Dassault design that eventually became one of the IAF’s most important platforms.
It also demonstrates that rejecting an aircraft does not necessarily mean rejecting its manufacturer permanently. Dassault’s subsequent success with the Mirage 2000 showed that India’s procurement decisions could be reassessed when a new aircraft offered a substantially different capability.
The Jaguar ultimately fulfilled the DPSA requirement, while the Mirage 2000 eventually found its own niche as a highly capable multirole fighter.

morning.text:
India and China could be among key players who could contribute to resolving the West Asia conflict if US President Donald Trump wants to use “diplomacy instead of bluster”, said former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Talking about the conflict, Clinton, in an interview with C-SPAN, said: “The misconceptions on a strategic level have led us to where we are.” The conflict began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched a joint attack on Iran, triggering retaliatory strikes. It also led to the choking of the vital Strait of Hormuz. In June, the US and Iran signed an interim peace agreement, but it collapsed last month with fresh strikes from both sides.

“China is far ahead of that; they have been banking a lot of fossil fuels they got in tankers … they have been building more reserves … but they are going to need Iran,” she said.
“It does seem to me that’s where the best pressure would come from if Trump were willing to actually use diplomacy instead of bluster,” Clinton said.

China, Turkiye and the UAE are Iran’s largest trade partners.

morning.title: Experts react to ex-CDS Chauhan’s remarks on Kirana Hills incident during Op Sindoor
morning.text:
Major General Dhruv C Katoch (Retd.), former diplomat KP Fabian and Foreign Affairs expert Waiel Awwad have offered detailed reactions to former Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General Anil Chauhan’s recent clarification regarding a possible strike on Pakistan’s Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor.
Former CDS General Chauhan had said that India did not deliberately target the site, which is associated with nuclear facilities, and that a loitering munition searching for radars near Sargodha may have inadvertently hit one of the hills after running out of operational time.
Major General Katoch described former CDS General Chauhan’s remarks as highly revealing.
“It gives out the fact that India did not have an intent to hit at the Kirana Hills,” he said.
Katoch recalled that during the post-strike conference held after the May 10 developments, Air Marshal Bharti had clearly said that the aim was not to hit the hills.
He emphasised that this established India’s stated position at the time.
“Regardless of the fact whether India intended to or did not intend to hit at the Kirana Hills, Kirana Hills was hit. And it was hit very, very accurately,” Katoch added.
According to him, the precision of the impact was significant.
He also noted that it was only after this incident that the United States became very concerned and active.
“Prior to that, the United States was not really interested in the war which was going on between India and Pakistan,” Katoch said, suggesting that the development near a sensitive site altered external perceptions and involvement.
Former diplomat KP Fabian said the statements by former CDS General Chauhan and Air Marshal Bharti need to be read together for a complete understanding.
“What our military is saying is that there was a loitering drone which went to Sargodha, but it could not locate any target and it had limited energy, so it started wandering and wandered towards the Kirana Hills,” Fabian noted.
He pointed out that Pakistan might have interpreted the movement as a deliberate plan to attack the Kirana Hills, where nuclear weapons are believed to be stored either entirely or partly.
“So what the Indian military spokespersons are suggesting is that Pakistan got scared… and after that Pakistan asked for a ceasefire,” Fabian said.
He indicated that the Indian side has stopped short of stating this conclusion in explicit terms, leaving room for interpretation about the psychological impact on Pakistan’s decision-making.
Foreign expert Waiel Awwad said Pakistan had been attempting to stabilise relations with India and had been sending messages across through back channels.
Referring to the broader context of Operation Sindoor, he noted that India, while seeking to maintain deterrence against Pakistan, was also ready for any kind of eventuality.
“Having said that, I would say that India is determined that there be no question of Pakistan using its territory for any terrorist group to act against India,” Awwad said.
He linked the episode to India’s consistent stance on cross-border terrorism.
The reactions from Katoch, Fabian and Awwad have contributed to renewed discussion on the sequence of events during Operation Sindoor, the role of precision munitions, the interpretation of intent versus impact, and the wider diplomatic and strategic implications that followed the reported incident near Kirana Hills.

morning.title: Indian oil companies to avoid Iran-blacklisted vessels amid security risks
morning.text:
At least three Indian oil refiners and a global energy major plan to stop using vessels on Iran’s new blacklist, including for ship-to-ship transfers, due to security concerns, four sources with direct knowledge of the matter said this week.Tehran announced on Sunday a blacklist of 45 ships it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway for global energy supplies six months into the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran’s announcement appears designed to impede the so-called shuttle runs Gulf oil producers such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have undertaken with dedicated tankers to move oil from the Gulf through Hormuz for unloading through STS transfers in the Gulf of Oman onto ships to end-users.
The shuttle runs have kept alive oil flows from the West Asia that have been curtailed by Iran’s clampdown on shipping through the strait because of the war.
The named vessels could be fined, detained and have their cargoes confiscated, according to a post on social media website X from the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a new body set up by Iran to manage the strait.
“We will avoid our chartered vessels dealing or STS or anything to do with non-compliant ships for Middle Eastern cargoes,” said one of the sources, who works at an Indian refinery.
The sources declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the issue.
Some of the tankers Iran listed are owned or chartered by Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (ADNOC). The ships have been used for shuttling crude, refined products and liquefied natural gas (LNG) out of the Gulf for STS transfer off Fujairah in the UAE or Sohar, Oman, according to shipping data.
Saudi Aramco and ADNOC declined to comment.
Ana Subasic, a trade risk analyst at shiptracking firm Kpler, said the most compliance-sensitive buyers are expected to avoid these vessels moving forward, but the trade is more likely to reroute through alternative tonnage, counterparties or transfer locations than disappear altogether.
INTERNAL DISCUSSIONS
Several charterers and shipping firms are discussing internally whether to continue their STS operations or not and are evaluating Iran’s warning, multiple other trade and shipping sources said, with one of them, a Gulf crude buyer, saying it would be safer to buy oil on a delivered basis shipped to a final destination instead of free-on-board at STS locations in the Gulf of Oman.
Those sources also declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the matter.
“Our internal departments are still in discussion on how to proceed with crude deliveries from the Strait of Hormuz via ship-to-ship transfers in the long term,” said Formosa Petrochemical Corp President KY Lin.
Iran has previously attacked several of the tankers, including the Wedyan, Mombasa B and Al Bahyah.
Two of the 12 very large crude carriers on Iran’s blacklist were no longer giving their location through their automatic identification systems (AIS) by Tuesday after the list was released, while the rest have had their AIS transponders switched off for weeks.
“The key issue is contagion,” Kpler’s Subasic said.
“If Iran follows through on threats to penalize vessels that conduct STS transfers with blacklisted tankers, that should narrow the pool of willing shipowners, charterers and buyers, particularly among firms with material Gulf exposure, while increasing due-diligence requirements and potentially freight, insurance and risk premia.”

morning.title: Claims Swirl Around CIA Director’s Reason For Secret Moscow Visit, Nearly All Of Them Are Terrifying
morning.text:
Troubling new reports are emerging about CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow on Tuesday. All of the reports point to delivering a warning to Putin’s regime, while exactly the nature of that warning differ.

There have been growing concerns in Europe over expanding Russian aggression and specifically the possibility it could attack a NATO country to test the alliance’s resolve. There are also reports that Putin will drastically increase offensive operations in Ukraine due to the massive damage his country is now taking from long-range drone and cruise missile strikes, as well as failed peace talks. Reports even state that he is mulling the use of tactical nuclear weapon in order to stop these attacks and change the tide of the years-long conflict, a possibility which we will discuss more later in this piece. Iran, of course, is also a major issue, but it seems, at least based on reporting, it had taken a backseat to whatever the director was trying to accomplish in Moscow.

Wednesday evening, The Wall Street Journal reported that Ratcliffe was in Moscow to deliver a message to Putin not to attack NATO countries. His visit “followed new U.S. intelligence assessments, reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, that Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test the resolve of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization with a limited assault on an allied country in the next few years,” the newspaper noted. We have been reporting on major concerns over exactly this for weeks now.

U.S. officials “are concerned that Putin, squeezed in Ukraine and under pressure at home, could launch an assault ranging from a cyberattack to a small-scale land incursion, likely on a Baltic nation, the Journal added. 

“Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow on Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his time in the Russian capital, but he didn’t meet with Putin. Putin was briefed on the talks, Peskov said,” according to the publication.

Earlier on Wednesday, ABC News reported that an explosive drone found near an An-124-100 Ruslan (NATO reporting name Condor) cargo jet at Leipzig airport in Germany earlier this month “bore the hallmarks of devices typically employed by Russia’s Military Intelligence Directorate, the GRU.” The network cited a U.S. intelligence source.

“The U.S. official, who was briefed on the investigation into the alleged sabotage plot, said the explosives fitted to the drone as well as the structure of the lethal device were ‘typical’ of those used by Russia’s GRU,” ABC added. “This U.S. assessment was made in conjunction with German security and intelligence agencies, the source added.

Numerous Russian drone incursions and other actions have some European officials convinced that Putin is already waging so-called hybrid war against NATO, and has been doing so for some time.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump downplayed the Ratcliffe trip, which has sparked a wide range of speculation about its purpose.

The president called it “semi-routine.”

That statement is hard to square considering how rare having a CIA director rush to Moscow is. The last time this happened was just prior to the war in Ukraine breaking out into the destructive reality we see today.

As we noted earlier in this story, Putin is reportedly considering escalating attacks on Ukraine, including the possible use of tactical nuclear weapons, Bloomberg reported, citing “three people close to the Kremlin.”

“For now, Russia is weighing an intensification of powerful conventional ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, including the center of the capital, and infrastructure targets in other Ukrainian cities.”

At issue, Bloomberg suggested, is that negotiation “frameworks have all effectively collapsed, leaving the two warring sides back at square one.”

This comes as Ukraine is already reeling from constant attacks, especially ballistic missile strikes it can’t defend against because of the lack of Patriot interceptors.

Moreover, the Kremlin “has also abandoned reliance on what it believed was an understanding reached between Putin and Trump at their summit in Alaska last August,” Bloomberg noted.

You can see video from that encounter below.

Such a deal would have required the Trump administration to force Ukraine into giving up the eastern Donetsk region, a demand Kyiv has rejected as it continues to hold out against a Russian onslaught that has gained little ground.

The White House this evening pushed back on the notion that negotiations between Ukraine and Russia have reached an insurmountable impasse. A peace deal has been a major objective for President Donald Trump, who famously promised that he would end the conflict on his first day in office.

“The president wants this war settled so that the senseless killing ends,” a White House official told TWZ. “The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done.” 

The United States “continues to play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end,” the official added. “We are the only country in the world that can play that role.”

The level of current U.S. involvement in negotiations is unclear. Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to travel to Moscow after an eight-month break and to visit Kyiv for the first time, but no date has emerged for either trip, Bloomberg noted. Last week, Radio Free Europe reporter Alex Raufaglu stated on X that the pair’s trip to Ukraine was delayed, but not canceled, by ongoing Russian attacks on Kyiv.

Putin is not about to cave under economic pressure, Bloomberg suggested, citing its sources. Nor will he end hostilities as Ukraine continues to pound Russian refineries and logistics networks. These attacks are having a devastating effect on the Russian economy and creating increasing frustration among the populace.

As we noted yesterday, Ukraine’s long-range strikes have spurred Putin to allow the government to temporarily seize what it deems commercial critical infrastructure that is not sufficiently protected against such strikes. This follows Russia’s move earlier this year to allow private companies to purchase their own air defense systems to protect their own facilities.

On Wednesday, those attacks continued anew. Ukraine struck another e-commerce hub, causing widespread damage, Russian officials said.

“As a result of the Ukrainian drone strikes, a fire broke out at a Wildberries logistics center,” Tambov Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov stated on Telegram. “The area of the fire is over 100,000 square meters.”

Whether Putin actually does escalate attacks remains to be seen. With increased production of ballistic missiles and new ones from North Korea, he may have new means of sustaining conventional attacks. As for a nuclear one, he has constantly rattled that saber for years. As Bloomberg noted, in the past, there have been reports that China and India have frequently urged him to refrain from that steep climb up the escalation ladder.

We raised the question of Putin using tactical nuclear weapons on Ukraine several months after he launched his full-on invasion, asking the world’s top nuclear proliferation experts of the likelihood it would happen. You can read this feature here, but our expert’s sentiments were made long before Ukraine was picking apart Russia infrastructure on a daily basis, with a standoff weapons armada growing by the day.

So, while it isn’t exactly clear what was discussed in this meeting or its primary objective, none of the reported reasons are encouraging. Quite the opposite, they point to the possibility of a darker new phase in the Russia-NATO standoff.

The inside story on why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face
morning.text:
The models responsible for last month’s agent hack of Hugging Face had been inadvertently trained to cheat and to communicate with each other, according to an OpenAI technical report released today. The hack, which a group of agents undertook to find solutions for a cybersecurity test that they were stuck on, has confirmed some experts’ fears that AI models might take actions that defy human desires and expectations. 

Since the hack, OpenAI employees—as well as researchers at the AI evaluation nonprofit METR, which released its own report on the hack today—have worked to understand what went wrong and how similar missteps might be prevented in the future. OpenAI has already put some preventative measures in place based on what they discovered. But making sure AI models do what we want them to do, or “alignment,” remains a gnarly problem, and some of the root causes of the hack will take much longer than a month to resolve.

“It’s not something you can solve overnight,” says Kai Chen, who runs OpenAI’s alignment research team. “There are challenges we’ve been tracking for a very long time, and we’re now seeing them with much greater precision.”

The Hugging Face hack was a product of months of misbehavior from OpenAI agents, first as they were being trained and then as their abilities were being evaluated. This May, agents in training figured out how to use OpenAI’s infrastructure to communicate with one another and get support with difficult training tasks, including some that were impossible to solve without hacking or otherwise misbehaving. That “message board” was shut down.

Then in July, while being evaluated for their cybersecurity abilities, some models created a new message board. They were supposed to be isolated from the internet, but by working together they managed to get online, hack Hugging Face, and obtain solutions for the cybersecurity problems that had stumped them.

Based on their investigation, OpenAI researchers believe that events during the training phase led directly to the hack. “For almost every behavior that was worrisome at evaluation time, [we were able to] find some sort of associated behavior at training time that actually we think might have contributed to it,” says Eric Wallace, a member of OpenAI’s alignment research team. 

When models correctly solve problems during training, the behaviors that led them to that solution are reinforced, and they become more likely to engage in them in the future. So if a model completed a task in May after using the original message board, it became more likely to participate in a new message board later on. This phenomenon, where AI agents misbehave in ways that are reinforced during the training process, is known as reward hacking.

Reward hacking also helps to explain why the models worked so hard to make their way onto the internet. During its investigation of the incident, the OpenAI team found that, over the course of training, the models became more and more likely to probe their digital environment for weaknesses and use the tools at their disposal in unexpected ways—a sign that these behaviors were being gradually reinforced. By the time the models were facing tricky cybersecurity problems, they had learned that hacking was an effective way to achieve their goals.

These results suggest that the Hugging Face hack could have been avoided if the models weren’t rewarded for misbehaving during training. While researchers don’t yet know how to prevent reward hacking entirely, OpenAI is taking some steps toward mitigating its effects. The company will now look for signs of cheating in all frontier models during training by keeping an eye on their chains of thought—internal notepads where they sketch out their answers and plan their actions. 

This solution isn’t as much of a slam dunk as it might seem: In earlier research, OpenAI showed that punishing models that mention cheating in their chains of thought teaches them to keep their intentions hidden from researchers. But monitoring its models’ thinking does give OpenAI the chance to halt the training process and reassess its approach if models do start learning to reward hack.

If OpenAI stops reinforcing reward hacking in its models—and that’s a huge “if”—that would be a huge step forward. But it wouldn’t solve the alignment problem. The first time a model communicated with other agents or hacked its infrastructure during training, those behaviors had never been reinforced, so agent misbehavior can’t only be attributed to that reinforcement.

Jeffrey Ladish, director of the AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research, compares the agents to a human who commits their first financial crime. “It’s not like they had to do fraud before to figure out that fraud is an effective strategy, and you have the same problem with models,” Ladish says. “Alignment science needs to be understanding how model motivations get shaped, such that we can actually figure out how to get models to care about the consequences of their actions.”

OpenAI’s researchers do have a hypothesis for where some of the misbehavior originated. Before the models formed their first secret message board, they had been trained to communicate and coordinate with subagents—less powerful agents to whom a main agent can delegate tasks. 

That learned communication behavior could have transferred to this new setting. The METR report, which investigates the messages that the models sent to one another in detail, supports this hypothesis: One agent on the message board took charge and assigned tasks to the other agents, effectively treating them as subagents. OpenAI could try to prevent agents from secretly communicating with one another by not training this subagent behavior in the future, but that would make the models less useful. 

This tension between capability and safety is at the heart of what went wrong with the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI researchers also identified the models’ persistence as a key factor in the hack. 

When they were accidentally given unsolvable problems, the models didn’t give up; instead, they strove to find solutions by any means necessary. But persistence is also a virtue, of course, especially if we want agents that can undertake large amounts of difficult work independently.

OpenAI is working on giving models ways to alert humans if they are given impossible tasks. The problem of teaching models when they should deploy their abilities and when they should hold back, however, won’t be settled in a single postmortem. The training strategies that create superhuman coders—rewarding them when they successfully solve problems—might not work to teach models to use their skills judiciously and respect human desires and values.

“I think there’s a bunch of alignment science that still needs to be done where we can move past just using proxies for task completion,” says Ladish. “That will work to make models very capable, but I don’t think it will work to make them aligned.”

The Porsche 911 GT3 Touring punches above its weight class
morning.text:
The GT3 occupies a singular place in the 911 lineup. Whereas the range-topping Turbo S piles on power, technology, luxury, and all-weather capability, the GT3 has always pursued something more elemental: a lighter weight, more focus, and a finely honed setup that puts the driver at the center of the experience.

Porsche has expanded the GT3 formula since the model’s debut in 1999, adding the more extreme GT3 RS to the lineup in 2003 and the slightly more reserved GT3 Touring in 2017, along with the GT3 S/C earlier this year. While the concept behind the drop-top S/C requires some mental gymnastics to make sense of it, the Touring’s original premise was refreshingly simple: Take the standard GT3—including its naturally aspirated 4.0 L flat-six and track-tuned chassis—and replace the fixed rear wing with the deployable spoiler from the Carrera. The result is a subtler version of the homologation car that recaptures the classic 911 silhouette without giving up the hardware that makes a GT3 a GT3.

Fresh from its 992.2 mid-cycle update, the latest GT3 Touring sticks closely to that original design. Its 4.0 L flat-six still spins to 9,000 rpm and produces 502 hp (375 kW) and 331 lb-ft (449 Nm), sending its output exclusively to the rear wheels through either a seven-speed PDK dual-clutch automatic or six-speed manual gearbox. Massive brakes, rear-axle steering, a GT3-specific suspension, active sport exhaust, and plenty of other road course-oriented hardware remain standard.

morning.title: Xbox’s new disc-to-digital program gives physical games a digital future
morning.text:
For decades, console owners have faced a choice between the convenience of digital downloads and the permanence of physical game discs. Soon, Xbox owners will be able to get the best of both worlds for thousands of supported titles as part of a newly announced disc-to-digital program.

The program—announced today ahead of testing for Xbox Insiders starting August 31—will let players claim a "digital entitlement" for "most Xbox One and Xbox Series X disc-based games" simply by inserting the disc into a console and launching it. That game will then be playable completely digitally, without the need to ever insert the disc, as long as you (or a member of your family account) is logged in. The digital entitlement will also allow access to features like Xbox Play Anywhere (for play on PC) and Xbox Cloud Gaming, for supported titles.

Microsoft says that your physical disc will "continue to work exactly as it always has" after the digital entitlement is claimed. But before you get any ideas, the fine print on the announcement mentions that there is only "one revokable license per game disc," so if you resell that disc or loan it to a friend, that digital entitlement could be transferred to a new account when someone else puts it into their console.
